title: Assertion functions and exhaustive error handling
hook: Assertion functions tell TypeScript that after a check passes, a value has a narrower type — or that a function never returns normally because it always throws. Combined with exhaustive switch on error unions, you eliminate impossible states at compile time.

blocks.text: An **assertion function** is declared with `asserts condition` in its return type. When you call `assertIsError(e)` on `unknown e`, TypeScript narrows `e` to `Error` in all code after the call — but only if the function returns normally. If the assertion fails, the function throws (or calls `process.exit`), so the narrowed path is safe. A related pattern is **`asserts arg is Type`** on a parameter. The **`never` return type** on functions like `fail(message)` signals "this always throws" — useful for exhaustive switch default branches and impossible cases.

entries.plainDefinition: Return type annotation that narrows a variable when the function returns without throwing.
entries.example: function assertIsString(x: unknown): asserts x is string

entries.plainDefinition: The empty type — no value exists. Used for functions that always throw or unreachable code.
entries.example: function fail(msg: string): never { throw new Error(msg); }

entries.plainDefinition: Compiler error when a switch on a union does not handle every member — often using never in default.
Function returning x is T — narrows in true branch only. Assertion functions narrow after the call regardless of branch.
entries.example: function isError(x: unknown): x is Error

blocks.text: Error handling code is repetitive — `if (!(e instanceof Error)) throw ...` at every site. A single `assertIsError(e)` centralizes the rule and keeps call sites clean. For discriminated error unions, an exhaustive `switch (error.kind)` with a `never` default means adding a new error kind forces compiler errors in every handler — the same safety Rust and C# pattern matching give you, but for TypeScript unions. Interviewers ask about assert vs type predicate: predicates narrow inside `if (isError(e))`; assertions narrow after the call on the same variable.

blocks.title: Assertions must throw on failure
blocks.body: If assertIsUser(x) returns without throwing when x is invalid, TypeScript still narrows — but runtime is wrong. Assertion functions are contracts you must honor.

diagram.title: Assertion and exhaustive error handling
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  U[unknown e] --> A[assertIsError]
  A -->|throws| FAIL[rethrow or wrap]
  A -->|returns| E[Error e narrowed]
  E --> MAP[to AppError union]
  MAP --> SW[switch error.kind]
  SW --> V[validation handler]
  SW --> N[not-found handler]
  SW --> T[timeout handler]
  SW --> DEF[default: never = err]
  DEF -->|new kind added| COMPILE[Compiler error missing case]

snippet.label: asserts vs type predicate
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–3: predicate returns boolean — narrow in true branch only. Lines 5–7: assertion throws on failure — narrows after call. Lines 14–16: assertIsError eliminates nested if at boundary.

snippet.label: never and fail for impossible branches
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–3: fail/never — always throws. Lines 14–21: default uses assertNever — if you add kind: 'triangle', default receives it and compile fails because triangle is not never.

snippet.label: Exhaustive AppError handler
snippet.explanation: Lines 14–17: assigning error to never in default — if a new kind is added to AppError, this default becomes a compile error. Safer than return 500 for unknown kinds.

blocks.title: Assertion that does not throw
blocks.body: function assertIsError(e: unknown): asserts e is Error { console.log(e); } — TypeScript narrows but runtime is unsafe. Always throw on failure.

blocks.title: default: return 500 without never
blocks.body: Swallowing new error kinds in a default branch hides bugs when AppError grows. Use const _: never = error to force updates.

blocks.text: Assertion functions are erased at runtime — they are thin throws with compile-time narrowing. Use them at trust boundaries after parsing JSON or catching unknown. assertNonNull is common with strictNullChecks. For discriminated unions, enable noImplicitReturns and prefer switch over if-else chains for exhaustiveness. In monorepos, shared assertIsDefined prevents duplicated guards. C# 11 switch expressions with when clauses achieve similar exhaustiveness at compile time; TypeScript needs never discipline. Production: when a new error kind ships, CI should fail on non-exhaustive handlers — tsc is your safety net. Do not use assertions for user input validation — use Result and return err; assertions are for programmer invariants and post-parse trust.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Confusing type predicate with assertion function narrowing scope. Using assert for user-facing validation. Not knowing never enables exhaustiveness. Saying assertions exist at runtime — they are compile-time contracts on throw behavior.

interviewTakeaways: asserts x is T narrows after the call; x is T predicate narrows only inside if.
never in switch default forces compile errors when error unions grow.
assertIsError centralizes unknown catch handling — throw on failure or the contract lies.
60s: Assertions are compile-time contracts that throw on failure. never for exhaustive AppError switch. Not for user validation — use Result. C# has catch filters; TS has asserts.
Follow-up: difference between assertIsDefined and optional chaining?
commonPitfalls: Assertion function that returns without throwing — unsafe narrowing.
default: return 500 instead of never — new error kinds slip through silently.
Strong answer: 'asserts at trust boundaries, Result for validation, never default in switch, assertNever for impossible.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS developers throw on failed invariants manually. TypeScript asserts documents which checks narrow types for the compiler.
C# switch expressions can be exhaustive over types and enums. TypeScript achieves similar safety with discriminated unions and never.
